body.text: In short:
Electricity transmission service provider ElectraNet is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula.
The company spent $300 million on a network upgrade which it said would provide more reliable power.
What's next?
ElectraNet says the transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time".

The owner of South Australia's high-voltage transmission network is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula, after pledging a $300 million network upgrade would provide more reliable power.

ElectraNet, the state's monopoly provider of electricity transmission services, has attributed the blackout to a "very unique, very rare" weather event that, at around 2.30pm on Thursday, damaged three transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula.
The downed towers were located at Wharminda, a small rural locality that sits along a 270-kilometre transmission line between Port Lincoln and Cultana.
ElectraNet spent $300 million on the high-voltage line, constructing 500 new transmission towers and upgrading five substations.
The project, named Eyre Peninsula Link, was completed in March 2023.
In a media release heralding its opening, ElectraNet CEO Simon Emms said it would give "residential and business electricity users a more secure and reliable power supply".

But the blackout that unfolded over Thursday afternoon and into Friday left ElectraNet fielding uncomfortable questions from residents, cabinet ministers and the media about how an outage of this scale could still happen.
ElectraNet executive Alex Trento was peppered with questions at a state government press conference on Friday morning.
But when asked whether he would be having a conversation with the premier about more funding, Premier Peter Malinauskas stepped in.
"This is a private company and a private operator that runs a healthy profit for their shareholders,"
Mr Malinauskas said.
"This is not a question for us. That's a question for them."
Earlier in the day, Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis struck a similar tone.

"There'll be a lot of questions after this is all over about how these over $300 million worth of upgrades on the Eyre Peninsula just three years ago — that we've all paid for in our power bills — have failed, and what was the weather event that caused them," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.
ElectraNet confident in transmission tower strength
ElectraNet is of the "strong belief" that the wind that hit the transmission towers was more than 172km/h.
That would be above the winds they were built to withstand under Australian engineering specifications.
Those specifications, Mr Trento said, were strengthened in 2016 following South Australia's statewide blackout.

While a structural fault could not be ruled out, Mr Trento said: "At this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively".
As to whether the engineering standards would need to be strengthened again, he said he had to wait for all the facts to be available.
"We could have been looking at a 215km/h hour wind event, we just don't know," Mr Trento said.
"So, until we have all that information, I really can't answer that question on whether the standards need to be updated."
The transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time", Mr Trento added.
"Unfortunately, you can never guarantee that the transmission network will not be subject to these extreme weather events."
'It all comes down to cost'
The blackout has also put renewed attention on the relationship between ElectraNet and the Australian Energy Regulator (AER).
The regulator has the final say on what transmission companies can spend on big infrastructure upgrades, balancing this with what they will need to raise from higher energy bills.
In September 2020, it gave ElectraNet approval to spend $280 million on Eyre Peninsula Link.
Mr Trento said a "secondary circuit" — which could have provided a redundancy to Thursday's blackout — was explored when ElectraNet was putting forward Eyre Peninsula Link.
"But that would have been double the cost, and that cost eventually ends up with the mums and dads of South Australia," he said.
Mr Trento conceded that the yet-known cost of repairing the damaged infrastructure would also have to come through consumer energy bills.
But he said that was "nowhere near the cost of adding a second line", which he estimated at $600 million.
"It all comes down to cost," he said.
"We can make things as big as we want to, and it will be like a Colosseum, and it will stand 2,000 years.
"But that's not efficient or prudent spending and will never get approved by the AER."
'We're not a third-world country'
Meanwhile, residents on the Eyre Peninsula are doing their own cost counting.
Port Lincoln business owner Jan Regan had to close her hearing care provider on Thursday afternoon, after losing all computer access and capacity to do hearing aid repairs.
She questioned how a $300 million transmission line could fail within years of its construction.
"Was it money well spent? Probably not, if you spend that much and it fails," she said.
"We're not a third-world country. I don't quite know what's happening, but it needs to be looked at."
